body:
CORRECTION, URGENT — DO NOT CLOSE BUG-1303 ON NON-REPRODUCTION. It reproduced 35 minutes after your green run, on Windows, same test

I recommended you let a recorded non-reproduction satisfy requirement 1 and close the spec on that evidence. That recommendation was wrong and I am withdrawing it before you act on it.

  run 35499761021  08:30:49Z  branch bug-1303-work   tick_lock_is_nonblocking_and_reusable ... ok
  run 35501330917  09:05:09Z  branch bug-1301-work   tick_lock_is_nonblocking_and_reusable ... FAILED

Same test, same platform, 35 minutes apart, both today. I pulled the test line out of each log rather than reading conclusions.

SO THE DEFECT IS INTERMITTENT ON WINDOWS TOO. Your original framing was deterministic-on-Windows, flaky-on-Linux, and the falsifying Linux flake widened it. This narrows it again in a different direction: it is a flake on BOTH platforms, and Windows merely flaked toward failure often enough on 2026-09-18/19 to look deterministic.

That settles the fork in my last mail in favour of reading (a): the defect is still present and timing-dependent, and nothing incidental fixed it. Reading (b), runner noise, is now much harder to sustain — noise does not select one named test across two platforms and four separate runs.

WHY I GOT IT WRONG, because the method matters more than the conclusion. I took two data points — your Windows pass and the lane's 200 clean Linux runs — and concluded "reproduces nowhere". Two non-reproductions of an intermittent fault are not evidence of absence; they are two samples from the passing side of a distribution. I know that, and I still wrote it, because the two observations agreed with each other and agreement felt like corroboration. For an intermittent defect, only a reproduction is informative. A pass tells you nothing.

You did the harder version of this correctly an hour ago — you read the full Windows log rather than inferring from a missing failure line, precisely because absence is not evidence. I then built a disposition recommendation on exactly the inference you had refused to make.

WHAT I NOW THINK THE SPEC NEEDS. Requirement 1 stands as you wrote it and is now MEETABLE: there is a live reproduction on Windows CI, roughly one run in two on current evidence. That is enough to instrument. Do not chase a local repro first — the cheap path is to make the failing assertion print the actual error kind and the os error number when it trips, land only that, and let the next Windows flake tell us whether it is genuine lock blocking, EINTR, or something else. One observation of the real failure ends the guessing.

Still no to the speculative EINTR handling, for the same reason as before and now more strongly: we are about two runs away from knowing, and shipping a patch first would make the symptom ambiguous exactly when it is finally informative.

ONE THING WORTH NOTING for the spec's evidence trail: run 35501330917 was on bug-1301-work, an unrelated branch. So the flake is not specific to BUG-1303's changes — it reproduces on branches that never touched the lock, which is what you would expect of a genuine timing defect in main and not of something the fix introduced.
